rows.stem: Which of the following belongs to the class of alkyl halides ?
rows.solution:
The alkyl halide is \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}Cl}\), 4-chlorobut-1-ene.

An ALKYL halide has its halogen on an \(sp^3\) carbon that is NOT next to a double or triple bond. Test each structure on where the chlorine sits.

\(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}Cl}\) has the chlorine on the \(sp^2\) carbon OF the double bond — that is a VINYLIC halide.

\(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}CH(Cl){-}CH_3}\) has it on the carbon NEXT TO the double bond — an ALLYLIC halide. \(\mathrm{CH{\equiv}C{-}CH_2{-}Cl}\) is the same arrangement with a triple bond.

In the remaining compound the chlorine sits TWO carbons away from the double bond, far enough that the \(\pi\) system has no influence on it, so it behaves as an ordinary primary alkyl halide.

The distinction matters because reactivity differs enormously. A vinylic halide barely undergoes nucleophilic substitution at all, its carbon-halogen bond being shortened and strengthened by resonance; an allylic halide reacts very readily, its carbocation being resonance stabilised; an alkyl halide sits between the two.

rows.stem: For the conversion of propene into 1-propanol, which of the following reagents and conditions should be used ?
rows.solution:
Use DIBORANE followed by alkaline hydrogen peroxide — HYDROBORATION-OXIDATION:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{B_2H_6}} (\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2})_3\mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O_2}/\mathrm{OH^-}} 3\,\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\)

The product wanted is PROPAN-1-OL, with the hydroxyl on the TERMINAL carbon — which is ANTI-MARKOVNIKOV, and that is what decides the reagent.

The boron atom, being the electron deficient partner, attaches to the LESS substituted carbon of the double bond, and the hydrogen to the other. Oxidation then replaces the boron by a hydroxyl with the geometry unchanged, so the hydroxyl ends up where the boron was.

The other three options are all acid-catalysed hydrations, which proceed through a carbocation and therefore follow MARKOVNIKOV'S RULE. Each would give propan-2-ol, since the secondary cation is the one that forms.

rows.stem: Which of the following reagents would one choose to transform \(\mathrm{CH_3COCl}\) into acetone ?
rows.solution:
Use DIMETHYLCADMIUM, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{Cd}\):
\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3COCl} + (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{Cd} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} + \mathrm{CdCl_2}\)

The difficulty in this conversion is STOPPING at the ketone. An acyl chloride is more reactive than the ketone it gives, so a strong nucleophile attacks the product as fast as it is formed.

That is exactly what a Grignard reagent does: methylmagnesium bromide would add TWICE, giving 2-methylpropan-2-ol rather than acetone. The dialkylcadmium is much the milder reagent — reactive enough to attack the acyl chloride, not reactive enough to attack the ketone — so the reaction halts at the right stage.

Chloromethane is not a nucleophile at all, its carbon being the electrophilic end.

rows.stem: The reaction of ammonia with a large excess of methyl chloride will yield mainly :
rows.solution:
The main product is TETRAMETHYLAMMONIUM CHLORIDE.

Alkylation of ammonia does not stop cleanly at one stage, because each product is a BETTER NUCLEOPHILE than the starting material. Alkyl groups release electron density, so every substitution leaves the nitrogen more nucleophilic and more eager to react again:
\(\mathrm{NH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CH_3Cl}} \mathrm{CH_3NH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CH_3Cl}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{NH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CH_3Cl}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{N} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CH_3Cl}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_4\mathrm{N^+Cl^-}\)

With methyl chloride in LARGE EXCESS the sequence runs to the end and gives the quaternary ammonium salt, in which the nitrogen holds four methyl groups and can react no further.

An excess of AMMONIA instead would give mainly the primary amine, each molecule of alkyl halide being far more likely to meet ammonia than a product amine. The proportions decide the outcome, not the reagents.

rows.stem: In the ring structure of glucose, the anomeric carbon is :
rows.solution:
The anomeric carbon is C-1.

When the open chain form of glucose closes into a ring, the hydroxyl at \(\mathrm{C_5}\) attacks the ALDEHYDE carbon, which is \(\mathrm{C_1}\). That carbon was planar and \(sp^2\); it becomes tetrahedral, and the new hydroxyl can point either way.

The two arrangements are the \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) forms — ANOMERS, differing at that one centre — so \(\mathrm{C_1}\) is called the ANOMERIC carbon.

Its distinctive chemistry follows from the ring being able to open again. That hydroxyl is HEMIACETAL rather than ordinary alcohol, so glucose still reduces Tollens' and Fehling's reagents, and a fresh solution slowly changes its optical rotation as the two anomers equilibrate through the open chain — MUTAROTATION.

Deficiency of the B vitamins causes BERI-BERI.

Beri-beri is specifically the deficiency disease of VITAMIN \(\mathrm{B_1}\), thiamine. It affects the nerves and the heart, and it appeared historically where polished rice was the staple, the husk removed in polishing being where the thiamine sat.

Each of the other options belongs to a different vitamin, and the set is worth holding together. Rickets is vitamin D, the bones failing to calcify. Scurvy is vitamin C, the connective tissue weakening so that gums bleed. Muscular weakness is associated with vitamin E.

The B group has several members with their own deficiencies — \(\mathrm{B_2}\) gives cheilosis, \(\mathrm{B_6}\) convulsions, \(\mathrm{B_{12}}\) pernicious anaemia — but beri-beri is the one named for the group in this question.

rows.stem: The cathode reaction during the charging of a lead storage battery leads to the :
rows.solution:
[This question has NO correct option, and the marking scheme says so explicitly, awarding the mark for any answer given. What follows is the chemistry it was reaching for.]

CHARGING REVERSES the discharge reactions. During charging the cell is driven as an ELECTROLYTIC cell, and at the CATHODE — the electrode where REDUCTION happens — lead sulphate is reduced back to LEAD:
\(\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)}\)

At the ANODE, simultaneously, lead sulphate is OXIDISED to lead dioxide:
\(\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + 2e^-\)

Now test the four options. Forming \(\mathrm{PbSO_4}\) is what happens on DISCHARGE, not on charging. Reducing \(\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}\) to \(\mathrm{Pb^{4+}}\) is self-contradictory — raising an oxidation state is oxidation, and it belongs to the anode. Forming \(\mathrm{PbO_2}\) AND \(\mathrm{Pb}\) describes the cell as a whole, both electrodes together, not the cathode alone. Depositing \(\mathrm{Pb}\) names the right substance at the WRONG electrode.

The answer the question needs — formation of lead at the cathode — is not among the choices.

rows.stem: Which one of the following pairs will **not** form an ideal solution ?
rows.solution:
NITRIC ACID AND WATER will not form an ideal solution.

An ideal solution requires the interactions between UNLIKE molecules to be essentially the SAME as those between like ones, so that mixing changes neither the volume nor the enthalpy. That holds when the two components are chemically similar — benzene with toluene, hexane with heptane, ethyl chloride with ethyl bromide, each pair being close relatives.

Nitric acid and water are not similar at all. Water molecules hydrogen bond to each other, and nitric acid hydrogen bonds to water MORE STRONGLY still, besides ionising in it. The unlike interaction is the strongest one present, so the mixture shows a large NEGATIVE deviation from Raoult's law.

The evidence is the azeotrope: nitric acid with water forms a MAXIMUM BOILING azeotrope at about 68% acid, boiling at 393.5 K — higher than either pure component. No ideal solution does that.

rows.stem: The half-life of a reaction is doubled when the initial concentration is doubled. The order of the reaction is :
rows.solution:
The reaction is ZERO ORDER.

For a reaction of order \(n\), the half-life depends on the initial concentration as
\(t_{1/2} \propto [\mathrm{A}]_0^{\,1-n}\)

The observation is that DOUBLING \([\mathrm{A}]_0\) DOUBLES \(t_{1/2}\), so the half-life is directly proportional to the initial concentration:
\(1 - n = 1\), giving \(n = 0\)

The result makes sense from the rate law itself. A zero order reaction proceeds at a CONSTANT rate whatever the concentration, so twice as much material takes twice as long to consume half of it.

The contrast worth remembering is FIRST order, where \(1 - n = 0\) and the half-life is INDEPENDENT of the starting concentration — which is why radioactive decay has a fixed half-life whatever the size of the sample. For second order the half-life would HALVE on doubling the concentration.

rows.subtopic: Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements
rows.stem:
Which of the following ions has the maximum number of unpaired d-electrons ?
[Atomic number : Fe = 26, V = 23, Ti = 22, Sc = 21]
rows.solution:
\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) has the maximum number of unpaired d electrons — FIVE.

Work out each configuration. The neutral atoms lose their \(4s\) electrons first, then as many \(3d\) as the charge requires:

Iron is 26, \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^6 4s^2\), so \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is \(3d^5\) — five orbitals, one electron each by Hund's rule, FIVE unpaired.
Vanadium is 23, so \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\) is \(3d^2\) — two unpaired.
Titanium is 22, so \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) is \(3d^1\) — one unpaired.
Scandium is 21, so \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) is \(3d^0\) — none at all, which is why scandium compounds are white and diamagnetic.

Five is the maximum any \(3d\) ion can reach, since a sixth electron must pair with one already present. That HALF-FILLED arrangement is also unusually stable, which is why \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is the stable state of iron and \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is so readily oxidised to it.

The magnetic moment follows: \(\mu = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = 5{\cdot}92\) B.M., the largest in the first transition series.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: Which of the following is a polydentate ligand ?
rows.solution:
\(\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}\) is the polydentate ligand.

The ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion binds a metal through SIX donor atoms at once — two nitrogens and four carboxylate oxygens — so it is HEXADENTATE and can wrap around an octahedral centre by itself, closing five chelate rings.

Ammonia is MONODENTATE, donating through its single nitrogen.

Ethylenediamine and the oxalate ion are BIDENTATE, each donating through two atoms. They do form chelates, but the term POLYDENTATE is kept for ligands offering SEVERAL donor atoms, beyond two — which is how the question separates them from the answer.

EDTA's grip is so tight that it is used to trap metal ions out of the way: it softens hard water by holding calcium and magnesium, and it is given medically to treat lead poisoning.

rows.stem: Which of the following coordination compounds exhibits linkage isomerism ?
rows.solution:
\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5NO_2](NO_3)_2}\) exhibits linkage isomerism.

LINKAGE ISOMERISM requires an AMBIDENTATE ligand — one that can bind through EITHER of two different atoms. The nitrite ion is the standard example, since both its nitrogen and its oxygen carry lone pairs:

Bound through NITROGEN it is the NITRITO-N (nitro) complex, \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]^{2+}}\), which is yellow.
Bound through OXYGEN it is the NITRITO-O complex, \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(ONO)]^{2+}}\), which is red.

Same formula, same atoms, different attachment — and a visible difference in colour.

None of the other three has an ambidentate ligand. Ammonia, chloride, carbonate and ethylenediamine each bind in only one way, so those complexes show other kinds of isomerism if any: facial and meridional for the first, optical for the last.

The other common ambidentate ligands are thiocyanate, binding through either nitrogen or sulphur, and cyanide, through either carbon or nitrogen.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) acts as a reducing agent.
Reason (R) : \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) state is stable due to \(\mathrm{3d^{5}}\) configuration.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

\(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is \(3d^6\); losing one more electron gives \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^5\) — an exactly HALF-FILLED d subshell, with every orbital singly occupied and the electron spins parallel. That arrangement is unusually stable, on two counts: the electrons are spread across all five orbitals so repulsion between them is least, and the exchange energy of five parallel spins is at its maximum.

So iron(II) gives up that electron readily, and a species that readily gives up an electron is by definition a REDUCING AGENT — it reduces something else while being oxidised itself.

The Reason therefore does not merely accompany the Assertion; the stability of the \(3d^5\) ion is precisely WHY iron(II) reduces.

The practical consequence is familiar: a solution of an iron(II) salt slowly turns yellow-brown in air as atmospheric oxygen oxidises it, which is why such solutions are prepared fresh.

rows.stem:
Give the structures and IUPAC name of the products expected from the following reactions :
(a) Reaction of methanal with \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}MgBr}\) followed by hydrolysis.
(b) Reaction of phenol with \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) (aq).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — in (a) the Grignard reagent is printed as a DRAWN hexagon bonded to \(-\mathrm{MgBr}\), and the ring is PLAIN: no inner circle and no Kekulé double bonds, checked at 2.6x magnification. That makes it CYCLOHEXYL, not phenyl, and the marking scheme confirms it by answering 'Cyclohexylmethanol'. I have named it losslessly as \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}MgBr}\) rather than describing the drawing, because the question asks for the PRODUCT and naming the reagent does not state it. Marked REQUIRED rather than ILLUSTRATIVE because the plain-vs-Kekulé distinction is the whole identity of the compound, is easy to misread, and the same question appears in the opener set 56/3/1 with a different reagent entirely. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) A Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon, and METHANAL is the aldehyde whose two hydrogens leave the product a PRIMARY alcohol, one carbon longer than the reagent:
\(\mathrm{HCHO} + \mathrm{C_6H_{11}MgBr} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_{11}CH_2OMgBr} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_{11}CH_2OH}\)

Structure: a cyclohexane ring carrying \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\).
IUPAC name: CYCLOHEXYLMETHANOL

(b) Bromine in AQUEOUS solution brominates phenol at all three activated positions at once, the hydroxyl group being strongly ortho, para directing:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + 3\mathrm{Br_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_2Br_3OH} + 3\mathrm{HBr}\)

Structure: a benzene ring carrying \(-\mathrm{OH}\) with bromine at positions 2, 4 and 6.
IUPAC name: 2,4,6-TRIBROMOPHENOL, which separates as a white precipitate.

The SOLVENT is what decides this. In a non-polar solvent such as carbon disulphide at low temperature, only ONE bromine goes on, and the product is mainly 4-bromophenol.

rows.stem:
The half-life of a first order reaction is 60 minutes. How long will it take to consume 90% of the reactant ?
[Given : log 2 = \(0{\cdot}3010\), log 3 = \(0{\cdot}4771\), log 10 = 1]
rows.solution:
The reaction is FIRST ORDER, so begin from the half-life:
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{k}\), giving \(k = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{60}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

If 90% is consumed, 10% REMAINS — so taking the initial amount as 100, the amount left is 10:
\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\)
\(\dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{60} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{100}{10}\)

Since \(\log 10 = 1\),
\(t = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303 \times 60}{0{\cdot}693}\)

\(t = 199{\cdot}3\ \mathrm{min}\), a little over three and a quarter hours.

A quicker route uses half-lives directly. Consuming 90% means the amount falls to a tenth, and
\(\dfrac{t}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{\log 10}{\log 2} = \dfrac{1}{0{\cdot}3010} = 3{\cdot}32\)
so the time is 3.32 half-lives — a little over three, which is the check on the arithmetic, since three half-lives would leave 12.5% and four would leave 6.25%.

rows.stem: What type of deviation from Raoult's law is shown by a mixture of ethanol and acetone ? Give reason.
rows.solution:
Ethanol and acetone show a POSITIVE deviation from Raoult's law.

In PURE ethanol the molecules are extensively HYDROGEN BONDED to one another, each hydroxyl hydrogen attaching to a neighbouring oxygen, and that network holds them in the liquid.

Acetone has no hydroxyl hydrogen, so it cannot join that network. When it is added, its molecules get BETWEEN the ethanol molecules and BREAK the hydrogen bonds without replacing them with anything as strong.

The ethanol molecules are then held less firmly than they were in the pure liquid, so their ESCAPING TENDENCY RISES, the partial vapour pressure of each component exceeds what Raoult's law predicts, and the total vapour pressure is higher than the ideal value.

The accompanying signs follow: breaking bonds costs energy, so mixing is ENDOTHERMIC and the mixture COOLS; and the volume INCREASES. Such a mixture forms a MINIMUM BOILING azeotrope.

rows.stem:
Give reasons :
(a) Formic acid is a stronger acid than acetic acid.
(b) Alpha \((\alpha)\)-Hydrogens of aldehydes and ketones are acidic.
rows.solution:
(a) Because the METHYL GROUP in acetic acid RELEASES electron density towards the carboxylate group, and formic acid has no such group.

The strength of a carboxylic acid is decided by how stable the ANION left behind is. Anything that spreads the negative charge out stabilises the anion and strengthens the acid; anything that concentrates it does the reverse.

Acetic acid's methyl group pushes electron density in by the \(+\mathrm{I}\) effect, INTENSIFYING the negative charge on the acetate ion and destabilising it. Formic acid carries only a HYDROGEN there, which has no such effect, so the formate ion is the more stable of the two and formic acid the stronger acid — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 3.75 against acetic acid's 4.76.

The same reasoning continues down the series: propionic and butyric acids, with larger alkyl groups, are weaker still.

(b) Because the CARBANION left behind is stabilised by RESONANCE with the carbonyl group.

Removing an \(\alpha\) hydrogen leaves a negative charge on the carbon next to the carbonyl. That charge does not stay there: it is delocalised onto the carbonyl OXYGEN, which is far better able to carry it, being the more electronegative atom:
\(\mathrm{{}^-CH_2{-}CH{=}O} \longleftrightarrow \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}O^-}\)

The resulting anion is the ENOLATE, and its stability is what makes the \(\alpha\) hydrogen acidic — it is removed by a base far more readily than a hydrogen on an ordinary alkane, although a carboxylic acid's hydrogen remains much more acidic still.

This acidity is the basis of the ALDOL CONDENSATION, in which the enolate of one molecule attacks the carbonyl carbon of another — which is why an aldehyde with no \(\alpha\) hydrogen undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction instead.
